00. Overview & Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate acute vs. chronic low back pain (LBP)
  • Describe the various types of pain and their associated causes
  • Recognize red flag symptoms and their associated conditions
  • Recognize anatomical structures; understand the basic mechanics and forces of the lumbar spine and the pathologies that can lead to LBP
  • Describe dermatomes and myotomes related to back pain
Required reading: Foundations of Osteopathic Medicine, 4th ed., pp. 325–347, 1112–1123, 1292–1295, 1427–1439; Osteopathic Medicine: A Core Concepts Approach, 1st ed., Ch. 5, pp. 59–71. Recommended: An Osteopathic Approach to Diagnosis and Treatment, 4th ed., pp. 241–248.

01. Epidemiology & Burden of Low Back Pain

  • In the U.S., low back pain ranks first among 154 conditions in healthcare spending — about $134.5 billion
  • Global Burden of Disease 2019: LBP is the single leading cause of disability worldwide
  • LBP is the leading cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) worldwide at 63.7 million — compare to diabetes (38.6 million) and COPD (30.6 million)
  • One of the most common reasons for missed work
  • Back pain is the 2nd most common reason for a PCP visit, second only to upper respiratory infection
The good news: acute and subacute LBP has a favorable natural history — in most reported series, the large majority of patients regain function within 6–12 weeks, with or without physician intervention.

02. Acute vs. Subacute vs. Chronic vs. Recurrent LBP

CategoryDurationKey Features
Acute< 6 weeksConnective tissue healing occurs; favorable prognosis — ~60% recover in 6 weeks
Subacute6–12 weeks80–90% recover in 12 weeks
Chronic> 12 weeks (3 months)Often attributed to degenerative or traumatic spinal conditions; connective tissue healing has already occurred; poor prognosis and increased disability — of those disabled >6 months, fewer than half return to work
Recurrence—40–50% of patients have a recurrence within the first 6 months; 70% within 12 months. Most recurrences still carry a favorable prognosis
Practice Question

03. Types of Back Pain

  • Pathology in the back typically causes limitation of movement in the affected spinal region
  • Patients often cannot differentiate whether pain is coming from bone, muscle, joint, or a neighboring structure
  • The reflex reaction to back pain is splinting of the involved segments via muscle spasm — this further blurs the patient's ability to localize the pain
Pain TypeCause / Origin
Radiating painSpinal nerve injury, mediated through the proximal spinal nerves — compression via disc herniation, osteophyte/bone spur, or a space-occupying lesion; leads to local edema, ischemia, and inflammation
Localized painArises from intraspinal structures — blood vessels, dura mater, and the longitudinal ligaments
Non-localized, non-radiating painArises from muscle, bone, and ligament outside the spinal canal
Referred painCan arise from abdominal viscera (aorta, pancreas, duodenum, colon, rectum, kidney, ureter, bladder, pelvic organs) or from systemic illness
Practice Question

04. Differential Diagnosis Categories & Clinical Evaluation

Three categories of LBP

CategoryApprox. frequency
Mechanical low back pain (bone, muscle, ligament)97%
Non-mechanical spinal condition1%
Non-spinal / visceral disease (visceral-somatic)2%

Clinical evaluation — history drives the exam

  • Get a thorough traditional history: location, quality, grade, radiation, history of presenting illness, mechanism of injury
  • Also gather a functional history — current work status and activity level. Key question: "What would you normally be doing that you can't do, or are avoiding, because of this problem?"
  • By the end of the history, you should already have one or several possible diagnoses in mind — the exam exists to explore those possibilities

Three diagnostic questions

  1. Do the presenting symptoms reflect a visceral disorder or a serious/life-threatening illness requiring imaging or further workup? (Screening for red flags)
  2. Where is the pain coming from?
  3. What is happening with this person as a whole that would cause the pain experience to develop and persist? (Biopsychosocial history — dynamic/passive instability, nociceptive system sensitization, psychological factors)

05. Red Flags: The 5 Serious Pathologies

The 5 most common serious pathologies to screen for in acute LBP:

PathologyKey red-flag findings
Vertebral fractureHistory of trauma; history of osteopenia/osteoporosis; history of long-term corticosteroid use
CancerPrevious history of cancer; unable to find a position of relief; fever; unexplained weight loss; blood in stool; pain in multiple sites
InfectionHistory of fever/chills; point tenderness; immunocompromised state; history of diabetes, UTIs, or IV drug use
Cauda equina syndromeBowel or bladder dysfunction (dribbling, inability to start/stop flow); saddle anesthesia (numbness/tingling anywhere that would touch a saddle)
Inflammatory arthritis (the "spondyloarthropathies")Psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis
Practice Question

06. Contraindications to HVLA

These do not necessarily prohibit soft-tissue, low-velocity, or low-amplitude procedures and mobilization — but are important considerations before performing HVLA.

07. Structure/Function Model of LBP Differential Diagnosis

Table 42A.8 from Foundations of Osteopathic Medicine organizes LBP differentials into 5 columns — red flags/spinal pathology, somatic dysfunction (mechanical, OMT-amenable), work-related/behavioral LBP, LBP radiating below the knee (neurological), and inflammatory/metabolic disorders — each broken down by history, physical exam, labs/x-ray, and course.

How to use this table: Somatic dysfunction (mechanical LBP amenable to OMT) classically presents as a well patient with mechanical, activity-dependent pain that does not radiate below the knee, nondiagnostic labs/imaging, and a good prognosis (90% recover from an acute attack in 6 weeks). Contrast this with radiating/neurological LBP (unilateral leg pain greater than back pain, positive reduced SLR, findings limited to one nerve root) or red-flag spinal pathology (age <20 or >55, violent trauma, constant progressive nonmechanical pain, systemic symptoms).
Practice Question

09. Bones, Ligaments & Vertebral Anatomy

  • 5 lumbar vertebrae, progressively enlarging from L1 to L5 — this helps transmit and support the load of the head, thorax, and upper extremities down the spine
  • Resists anterior gravitational movement by maintaining lumbar lordosis

Key structures

  • Superior + inferior articular processes combine to form the zygapophyseal (facet) joint — a common source of mechanical LBP
  • Facet joints in the upper lumbar spine lie more in the sagittal plane (favoring flexion/extension); further down the lumbar spine (toward L5–S1) they shift toward a more oblique/coronal plane (favoring side-bending and rotation)
  • Pars interarticularis ("isthmus"/"island of bone") — the bone between the superior and inferior articular processes. Under chronic traumatic stress it can fracture, producing the classic "Scotty dog" fracture on oblique X-ray (fracture line at the "collar" of the dog) — think spondylolisthesis
  • Intervertebral foramen — the space nerve roots exit through. Its size is dictated by disc height and pedicle shape. As discs lose height with degeneration, the posterior longitudinal ligament may hypertrophy and osteophytes/bone spurs may form — all of which narrow the foramen and can produce nerve root ("pinched nerve") symptoms

Ligaments

TypeExamplesNotes
Multisegmental (span multiple levels)Anterior longitudinal ligament, posterior longitudinal ligament—
Segmental (span one level)Interspinous, supraspinous, intertransverse ligamentsSupraspinous ligament provides the most resistance to flexion (connects tips of spinous processes); interspinous ligament runs oblique to the spine's compressive axis — functionally similar to knee collateral ligaments, helping guide flexion while limiting transverse/frontal motion

10. Muscles of the Back & Trunk

These muscles provide stability to the spine during dynamic movements and actions:

  • Latissimus dorsi
  • Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis)
  • Rotatores, multifidi
  • Internal obliques, transversus abdominis
  • Gluteus maximus, medius, minimus
  • Psoas, iliacus
  • Quadratus lumborum
  • Piriformis

11. Spinal Motion & Segmental Mobility

  • Spinal motion is the combination of the intervertebral joints and the facet joints
  • Reportedly 15–40% of LBP stems from the facet joints
  • Facet joints guide intervertebral motion through their plane orientation (frontal/sagittal/coronal) and help protect the disc from excessive twisting or hyperflexion, and help resist excessive rotation

Segmental mobility depends on:

  1. Vertebral body/disc size — disc height maintains alignment of joint surfaces and tension on the segmental supporting ligaments
  2. Facet orientation — sagittal plane (upper lumbar) favors flexion/extension; as the plane becomes more frontal/coronal (lower lumbar), more rotation and side-bending are allowed. Disc-space narrowing from degeneration changes the positional relationship of vertebrae to one another, adversely affecting joint mechanics

12. The Intervertebral Disc

  • Along with the bones, provides static stability
  • The largest avascular structure in the body

Annulus fibrosus

  • Composed of 10–20 layers of fibrocartilaginous fibers that insert onto the vertebral body
  • Houses nociceptors and proprioceptive nerve endings

Nucleus pulposus

  • Gelatinous mucopolysaccharide center, ~90% water — this water content decreases with age
  • Composed of a protein-bound chondroitin sulfate (proteoglycan) that gives the disc its hydrophilic/fluid-maintaining capacity
  • Provides extra strength during compression
  • Nutrition depends on diffusion of water — only the outer third of the disc has a blood supply
Aging pearl: As the disc dehydrates/degenerates, it loses its ability to develop internal fluid pressure and transform compressive loads into radial (hoop) force on the annulus fibrosus. This shifts more load onto the vertebral bodies themselves, driving further degenerative changes (osteophyte/bone spur formation) — i.e., degenerative disc disease leads to degenerative joint disease.

13. Innervation of the Lumbar Spine & Disc Herniation

Plexuses

PlexusRoot LevelsKey Nerves
Lumbar plexusL1–L4 (+T12); passes through psoas majorIliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator, femoral, + short direct muscular branches
Sacral plexusL4–S4; lies between piriformis and pelvic fasciaSciatic (common fibular + tibial divisions), superior & inferior gluteal, posterior cutaneous femoral, nerves to quadratus femoris/obturator internus/piriformis
Pudendal & coccygeal plexusS2–S4, S5–Co1Pudendal, perineal, dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris, anococcygeal
Remember: the spinal cord itself ends around L1–L2 (conus medullaris), but nerve roots continue down within the dural sac as the cauda equina.

Nerve roots & disc herniation

  • Nerve roots exit above the disc, through the foraminal opening
  • An L3 disc herniation affects the L4 nerve root (or below)
  • An L4 disc herniation affects the L5 nerve root (or below)
  • An L5 disc herniation affects the S1 nerve root (or below)
  • The most common disc herniations occur at L4–L5 and L5–S1

15. Facet Joint Dysfunction

  • Facet joints are lined with smooth cartilage and lubricated with synovial fluid
  • They guide intervertebral motion through their orientation in the transverse and frontal planes, and limit motion to protect the disc from excessive twisting/hyperflexion
  • These joints react to trauma and inflammation — producing pain, stiffness, and dysfunction, with secondary muscle spasm leading to further joint stiffness and degeneration
  • Reportedly 15–40% of LBP stems from facet joint involvement

16. Types of Segmental Loading & Forces

Four main types of segmental loading on the lumbar spine: axial compression, bending (flexion/extension), torsion (rotation), and shear (side-bending stresses are considered together with rotational stress in the summary below).

Axial compression

  • Caused by gravity, ground reaction forces, muscle contraction, or ligament reactions to tensile forces
  • Hoop stress: the disc tolerates compressive load by converting vertically applied compression into circumferentially applied tension
  • As compressive load increases pressure within the nucleus pulposus, that pressure is exerted radially against the surrounding annulus fibrosus
  • Most load is carried anteriorly (the thickest portion of the disc); the posterior disc can carry 0–30% of the load depending on segment/position — this is why most disc herniations are posterior or posterolateral (the weaker portion)

Bending (flexion and extension)

  • A combination of compression, shear, and tensile forces on the segment from translation
  • The nucleus pulposus tends to deform in the direction opposite the applied load
  • Flexion: NP deforms posteriorly; superior vertebra anteriorly tilts/forward glides; intervertebral foramen widens ~24%; anterior compression, posterior tension (posterior longitudinal ligament + supraspinous ligament); central canal widens. Segments are recruited superior-to-inferior (upper lumbar moves first)
  • Extension: NP deforms anteriorly; posterior disc sustains compressive force, anterior segment undergoes tensile loading; superior vertebra tilts/glides posteriorly; intervertebral foramen narrows ~20%; central canal narrows. Overall lumbar extension range is much less than flexion due to lumbar bony geometry (spinous processes approximate one another; anterior longitudinal ligament tension restricts motion)

Torsion

  • Caused by axial rotation and coupled motion
  • The disc is much less tolerant of torsional/rotational forces — annulus fibrosus fibers run obliquely, so during rotation only a portion of the fibers are under tension at any given time (limiting the disc's ability to resist torsional stress)
  • Facet joints help limit rotation and protect against these forces
  • When torsion is combined with flexion, the force required for tissue failure decreases significantly (classic mechanism: bending, lifting, and twisting — e.g., shoveling snow — is when the disc is most vulnerable)
Practice Question

17. Summary of Forces: Tissues & Injuries

ForceTissues ResistingTypical Injury
Compressive (axial) loadingVertebral bodies, intervertebral disc, abdominal mechanismVertebral body or endplate fracture
Rotational & side-bending stressFacet joints, pedicles, abdominal mechanism, quadratus lumborum, superficial & deep back musclesFracture of the pars interarticularis or pedicle
Flexion stressPosterior ligament system, posterior annulus fibrosus, thoracodorsal fascia, superficial & deep back musclesAnnular tear, disc herniation, muscle injury
Extension stressAnterior ligament system, posterior bony elements, abdominal mechanismPars fracture, traumatic spondylolisthesis
Protection of neurovascular elementsFibro-osseous foramina (intervertebral foramina)Entrapment of cauda equina and/or nerve roots
